pages.text:
Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Wednesday, 28 August 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 49)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney SC with Ms Emily Aitken for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning.
PROFESSOR MAY: Good morning.
MR GLOVER: Thank you, Commissioner, we convene this
morning to take some evidence from Professor Jennifer May,
who, as you will have now observed, is on the screen and
ready to go.
<JENNIFER ANN MAY, SWORN [10.02 am]
<EXAMINATION BY MR GLOVER
THE COMMISSIONER: Thank you, Mr Glover.
MR GLOVER: Professor May, can you see and hear me okay?
A. I can't see you. I can see the Commissioner, but
I can't see you. But I can hear you well.
Q. All right. Well --
THE COMMISSIONER: It's probably better off that way.
MR GLOVER: -- it's probably for your benefit that way,
yes. I think the Commissioner beat me to it.
A. Right, now I've got you.
THE COMMISSIONER: I'm kidding, but - yes.
MR GLOVER: I'm not. To the extent at any stage you can't
hear me or the connection breaks up, just let us know;
okay?
A. Thank you.
Q. Can you tell us your full name, please?
A. Jennifer Ann May, M-a-y.
Q. And you're currently the director of rural health at
the University of Newcastle; is that right?
A. I am. I live in Tamworth, northern New South Wales.
Q. Thank you. To assist the Commission in its work,
yesterday you made a statement; correct?
A. I did. Correct.
Q. For the benefit of the transcript, it's
[SCI.0011.0384.0001]. Now, if I take you to paragraph 28

of your statement. I understand there's a correction that
you would wish to make in relation to the document
described as annexure E; is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. What I'll do is I'll have the operator bring up on the
screen [SCI.0011.0393.0001], and hopefully in a moment,
Professor May, on your screen will appear a document. Can
you see that document?
A. It has, yes.
Q. And is that the document that should be annexure E?
A. Yes.
Q. Rather than the one that was originally attached to
your statement; is that right?
A. Correct. That's the document alluded to in that
paragraph. Thank you.
Q. And, other than that correction, is your statement
true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?
A. To the best of my knowledge.
THE COMMISSIONER: Does that mean I've got the wrong
annexure E?
MR GLOVER: Yes. The effect of that, Commissioner, is
that the annexure E that was originally attached has been
substituted for the document on the screen, and I'll hand
you a copy of the correct one for your exhibit.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thanks.
MR GLOVER: Commissioner, given that we only have a few
documents this morning, I tender the statement and the
annexures now. I'm told we are at exhibit M1.
THE COMMISSIONER: The folder I've got has gone up to
exhibit E.
MR GLOVER: Yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: Then there's some other documents.
MR GLOVER: Yes, those documents --
THE COMMISSIONER: No, annexure F, sorry. Annexure F.

MR GLOVER: It should go to G.
THE COMMISSIONER: G. Then there's a supply and demand
study for general practitioners.
MR GLOVER: Yes. That's not annexed to the statement, but
I'll be taking the Professor to it shortly.
THE COMMISSIONER: Right. Okay. So is that part of
the tender?
MR GLOVER: It will be, yes, but separately from the
statement.
THE COMMISSIONER: Got it. Okay. Thanks.
MR GLOVER: So I tender the statement and annexures now,
and I'm told that it should be marked exhibit M1.
THE COMMISSIONER: And the "Supply and demand study,
general practitioners in Australia, August 2024" will get a
separate exhibit number.
MR GLOVER: And, if convenient, I'll do it now as M2.
Q. Professor, you've got a copy of your statement there
with you?
A. I do.
Q. All right. And I'll start with paragraph - before
I do that, in paragraph 3 you tell us that you oversee the
rural health multidisciplinary training program?
A. Correct.
Q. Can you tell us a little bit about that program? What
does it involve?
A. Indeed. It's a Commonwealth-funded program that works
through education. So it's a grant program that is given
to universities by the Commonwealth Department of Health,
and it is to - I call it the gain, train, retain program,
but its specific intent is to affirmatively support rural
recruitment and return of health professionals. But it
does it through supporting university education and
training, and the development of infrastructure in rural
areas to support high-quality delivery of services.

Q. So, in terms of it being directed to rural recruitment
and return of health professionals, what sort of
initiatives does your program implement with that funding
to achieve that aim?
A. So as part of the Commonwealth KPIs of that program we
are asked and we happily ensure that up to 30 per cent of
the entrants into the joint medical program run by UON and
UNE are of rural origin. So one of the things we know is
predictive of rural return is rural origin. So there's a
30 per cent target there. But the majority of our program
is focused on I guess incentivising and affirming rural
training. So positive rural exposure of more than
12 months is a greater predictor of rural return. The
longer, probably the better, although the evidence around
more than two years is probably less clear at this point.
What we know is that rural origin and positive rural
exposure are synergistic in improving the chances of rural
return. But those two efforts on their own are clearly not
enough, and what is very evident is that multiple
strategies are always required if you are trying to
incentivise a certain outcome in your workforce. So a
concentration in postgraduate training and, if you like,
the opportunities that are beyond the remit of the
traditional from the medical school point of view are also
supported through this program. So the regional training
hub portion of the program works specifically at supporting
new medical officers in our regional areas and supporting
rural training and rural careers.
Q. Thank you. Could I take you to paragraph 6 of your
statement. There you tell us a little about the state of
the general practitioner workforce and some trends. Do you
see that?
A. Yes.
Q. And then in paragraph 12 you tell us that your view is
that:
The current health workforce, particularly
the general practitioner workforce, is
challenged to meet the needs of the New
South Wales population having regard to
current distribution patterns, population
growth and increasing service demand.
Do you see that?

A. I do.
Q. Can you just describe in general terms what those
challenges are as you see it?
A. So - and I think the GP supply and demand study also
alluded to this - what we see is insufficient inflows into
general practitioner training. We see some changing
demographics and workforce preferences, we see a reduction
in the number of hours, and we see demand for services
going faster than population growth.
In addition, in the rural context the expected scope
of practice of general practitioners is wider, and the
requirement and the need to provide procedural services
and, I guess, more thought of as secondary services within
our district hospitals is an additional role which
increases the number and the requirement for general
practitioners in rural areas. It is in that area in
particular that we've seen workforce challenge to this
point, and obviously where we've seen some initiatives of
recent times to try and redress that retention of that
specific workforce.
Q. And is this a trend that you have observed over a
relatively long period of time or has it accelerated in
recent years?
A. So it's a trend that's been observed over probably
40 years. There's evidence going back to 1987 of a
reduction in the proportion of general practitioners versus
other non-GP specialists being trained in our system. So
these are long-term trends, and they're not even just
Australian trends. These are international trends. So the
move away from generalism and towards specialism has been
longstanding.
The issue is that the impact of those trends in our
rural areas is greater, and so I think I would describe
rural as the canary in the coal mine in many ways in terms
of that trend and the impact, as I said, being
substantially greater on residents.
Q. Can I take you briefly to the supply --
THE COMMISSIONER: It's probably always been the case,
hasn't it, that a general practitioner that practises in a
regional and particularly in a rural area is probably - he
or she has always probably been required to have a more

expansive scope of practice than a city-based GP; correct?
A. Correct.
Q. Yes.
A. And I guess the acceptability and the attractiveness
of that skill set within our medical workforce has reduced
over time. So the attraction of specialism over that
generalism has reduced over time.
Q. Yes, but the clinicians in the regional centres have
consistently told us, I think, that it's - general practice
in rural, remote, regional areas is just a different form
of general practice than if you're a city GP because you're
going to be called upon to do a whole - just by dint of
there not being someone with specialisation available,
you're going to have to do a lot more procedures than you
would if you were a GP in Mosman or Edgecliff or Newtown?
A. Correct. And the other aspect of it is the number of
hours.
Q. Yes.
A. So whereas in a city practice you can close the door
or suggest that someone go down the street because you know
that there are options for them in terms of accessing care,
if you're one of a small number of practitioners in a rural
area, that's very difficult, particularly if you're living
where you're working.
Q. Yes.
MR GLOVER: Can I take you brief --
THE COMMISSIONER: And by dint of the population size
you're well known in the area?
A. And I do allude to that in my statement, and that is
one of the challenges in recruitment and retention, is the
drawing of professional and personal boundaries, and
obviously people differ in their comfort and often in their
life stages as to how well they can tolerate or would want
the sort of exposure that one necessarily gets.
Q. Yes.
MR GLOVER: Operator, can we bring on the screen, please,
the supply and demand study. It's [SCI.0011.0392.0001].
Can we just go to page 12 of that document, please,
internal page 12. I think the coding matches on this one.

THE COMMISSIONER: Could we go to page 8 first?
MR GLOVER: Yes, of course.
THE COMMISSIONER: Okay. That's not - at page 8. Yes,
that's the one. Could I just ask for your help, Professor,
in relation to these definitions of baseline demand and
unmet demand. So baseline demand is defined as the number
of GPs that are needed to meet the current and future
health needs of the community. How have the current and
future health needs of the community been defined or who's
determined that and how it that --
A. Indeed. I affirm your concern about that particular
statement or how it might have been --
Q. The reason I'm asking is it could be based on just
utilisation, but that may not reflect what the need is and
there might be - I mean, it really depends. If the current
and future health needs mean keeping the population with
the same general health as it has now, that might be one
thing. But if there's chronic disease in that community
and you want to reduce the rates, intervene earlier, have
people with average - spending average - a lower average
number of years with chronic disease or seek to prevent it
entirely, then the number of GPs might be - that are needed
might be higher?
A. I would heartily agree.
Q. Okay.
A. I think you'll see that sense where it actually
appears to be calculated on current GP service utilisation
levels --
Q. Yes, that's what I - where I've looked at unmet
demand, it uses that term "utilisation level". So I've
assumed that it's based on the people - data about how many
people are going to GPs, at what sort of frequencies. But
it may not be what's actually required if you want to, for
want of a better expression, promote the health of a
particular population. By "promote" I mean improve it.
A. And, Commissioner, if I could just add to that that
this calculation assumes that we are at, you know, a stable
one equals one state.
Q. Yes.
A. I would contend to you that in rural areas we are

significantly underdone.
Q. Yes.
A. And, as I've said, I've provided some circumstantial
evidence for that, like waiting times and access, because
measuring unmet need is very difficult. We can't go on
vacancy rates --
Q. Yes.
A. -- we can't - you know, there are real challenges
in --
Q. So by what you're saying there should I take it to
mean that utilisation levels in a particular population
where the GP market is thin is not the best guide?
A. I can affirm that observation.
Q. Okay. Thank you.
MR GLOVER: So is the effect of that exchange, Professor,
that you have some concern that the assessment of need
might not - might underrepresent actual need within the
community?
A. Correct.
Q. All right.
A. I understand that any of this methodological
calculations are fraught, and I applaud the authors for
having a go. But I think we need to question some of the
assumptions.
Q. On page 5 and 6 there is some detail concerning the
models used, and if one looks about halfway down the page
of page 5, the demand modules --
A. So this links to the Commissioner's concern about the
chronic disease and health service utilisation, which are
assumptions that they have tried to make in this modelling,
and, as I said, I would regard them as fraught. The
question is: is there a better question or a better way of
doing it? And certainly demand modelling - most people are
very uncomfortable about demand modelling. Far easier to
demand, supply or actual. But trying to model demand
particularly in the view of technological change, which
may - whilst making health service delivery more efficient,
technological change is offering us so many greater options
for the way we manage many of our illnesses or injuries,
and I do stroke prevention as a good example. We are now

looking at clot retrieval as one of the best practice
treatments for stroke. Well, clearly 10 years ago that was
not even in any demand modelling for the types of
professionals we might need if we were going to supply a
clot retrieval service. So I think it's just that real
challenge about how we model going forward in the demand
space.
I think my other concern is this idea that we're
starting in a steady state in 2024, where I believe there
are quite a lot of circumstantial evidence that suggest,
although we have a head count of general practitioners that
is greater than we had before, the actual capacity of
residents to access general practice services may not be as
good as it was, say, five to 10 years ago.
THE COMMISSIONER: I imagine - I mean, I'm not for a
moment suggesting this report isn't useful, but if you were
determined to produce a study about what might be needed
to - what might be needed in terms of the GP workforce
primary care health services to reduce the rates of chronic
disease and the length of time that the population suffers
from chronic disease, that would be a massive undertaking
to do that work, wouldn't it? It wouldn't be - it would be
a really long-term, difficult job with a huge amount of
time spent on the methodology that was going to be used and
the modelling that was going to be used?
A. Absolutely. And I guess it also goes to some of the
assumptions around access.
Q. Yes.
A. So this modelling doesn't take into - or the - some of
the issues around access include the acceptability of
access, the affordability of access and the availability of
access. So we're just thinking if there's a GP - if
there's, you know, a body that reports to APRA as a GP in a
certain residential area that that equates to access, and
I think there are some other factors that would need to be
considered when we were considering whether we were
undersupplied for population need.
Q. Sure. I guess my point is you can read any number of
Treasury or intergenerational reports that say we have to
intervene earlier and shorten the time that people suffer
from chronic disease if we're going to get - we're going to
reduce the rate of the growth in the budget spend on health
care, but if you're actually really determined to do that

then you've got to do the big, difficult study to work out
exactly how that would best be targeted and exactly what
levels of GP/primary care are likely to be needed to in
30 years time or 20 years time find out you have reduced
the rates of chronic disease and thereby prevented people
going to hospital and thereby reduced the growth in the
health spend?
A. Yes, I affirm that, Commissioner. Absolutely.
Q. Okay.
MR GLOVER: And part of that must include, must it not, a
detailed assessment of the likely health service needs of
the population both in the short, near and long term?
A. Yes. And I guess the challenge for us all is that
chronic diseases take 20 to 30 years to develop. So we're
actually coasting on the coattails of the health care we
received 20 to 30 years ago, and it's going to take that
long for potential lack of access to impact on some of
those - the incidence and prevalence of some of those
diseases.
Q. Accepting the concerns about the modelling, but
proceeding on the basis, I think I've understood you
correctly, that those concerns would lead to a conclusion
that the estimates in this study are conservative; have
I understood you correctly?
A. Correct.
Q. All right. If we go to page 12 - internal page 12,
thank you, Operator - and you'll see under the heading "New
South Wales" these are the New South Wales projections. At
the moment the baseline gap is around 230 FTE; do you see
that?
A. Yes.
Q. And one of the features of the changes in medical
practice, not only for general practitioners but across the
board, that you've told us about is changes in work
patterns that clinicians seek; correct?
A. Yes.
Q. And so it may be that one practitioner no longer, to
the extent it ever did, equates to one FTE?
A. Correct.

Q. So the number of practitioners to close that gap would
be - it would be reasonable to assume a lot or - I'll
withdraw that and start again. On that basis it would be
reasonable to assume that the number of practitioners
required to close the 230 FTE gap as it stands at the
moment would be higher than 230 clinicians; correct?
A. Indeed. I would qualify that, and there is a
qualification in this document that talks about a
difference between Australian-trained medical graduates and
their FTE and international medical graduates who come into
New South Wales on an obligatory pathway where their visa
dictates them being in a non-metropolitan area for a period
of time, and what we see is that those practitioners, and
understandably, will have a higher FTE while they're in
their obligated practice.
Q. For the benefit of the transcript, that qualification
appears on page 21.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thanks.
MR GLOVER: You'll then see on page 12, Professor, the
projected increase in the gap between baseline demand and
the number of clinicians available, and it increases rather
rapidly between now and 2028, and then between 2028 and
2048; do you see that?
A. I do.
Q. Do you have a view about the effect on the healthcare
system as a whole if that gap eventuates as predicted?
A. I expect that our models of primary care delivery will
need to change in order to make that figure, you know, not
the case. It is inconceivable to think that the system
could work well with an undersupply of 2300 FTE by 2048,
but it is my observation that there are a number of changes
occurring which will change the scope of practice and the
balance of activity within primary care that will need to
go some way to alleviating that sort of shortage.
Q. What are those changes that you're observing?
A. So currently there's a scope of practice review under
way with the Commonwealth government where allied health
professionals - well, scopes of practice are being
revisited to understand where there are complementary
scopes of practice or where primary care responsibility can
be shared and collaborated on across the health care team.
So there's a focus on multidisciplinary care. So one would

expect that with that focus on multidisciplinary care and
some sharing of the general practice workload that we would
be going some way to ameliorating that shortage.
Do I think that scope of practice is likely to
completely meet that level of unmet demand? I don't, and
the reasons for that are that our distribution of nurses is
not unlike our distribution of GPs, and our distribution of
other allied health professionals is also not unlike our
distribution of GPs. So this may be a solution in
metropolitan areas, but my concerns are that we're not
starting with a workforce that has huge excess capacity
that we could work with sharing the sorts of
responsibilities that we will need to if primary care is to
change.
Q. By distribution do you mean the maldistribution of
clinicians of all kinds --
A. Correct.
Q. -- heavily weighted towards metropolitan areas?
A. That's exactly what I mean.
Q. Although you have some reservations about how far it
will go, do we understand you, though, to be of the view
that having clinicians operate to the top of their scope of
practice wherever possible is one mechanism that may
alleviate some of the workforce challenges posed by
maldistribution?
A. I do, and that includes getting our rural GPs working
to the top of their scope and rural generalism and the
increased focus on training for rural generalism, and that
is extra scopes of practice - well, expanded scopes of
practice with obstetrics, anaesthetics, mental health,
paediatrics as well as a baseline in emergency is required
in order to deliver those services in a distributed
capacity.
THE COMMISSIONER: That scope of practice review I think
you've just touched on might not just recommend clinicians
working to the full scope of their practice but it might
recommend an expanded scope of practice for people with
skills that - where they could have an expanded scope of
practice with some change of legislation, for example?
A. Yes, I think that's a likely outcome.
Q. Yes. Is a greater utilisation - to the extent that

it's possible, a greater utilisation of virtual medicine,
virtual consultations, could that be a means of bridging
this gap between supply and demand?
A. Somewhat. But the thing that --
Q. Not as a complete answer, but as an aid?
A. Absolutely, and virtual care is already an important
part of health care delivery in rural and remote, and
I think it's - the way the models evolve it will have an
even greater role. What we've got to do is also when we're
thinking about these projections, in 2048 what is the
technological capacity going to be of our system? What
will health care look like? You know, I wonder whether we
will be interacting with a virtual care, artificially
intelligent assistant who will be monitoring by wearables
our various health --
Q. Yes.
A. So that system is going to interact differently with,
you know, the professionals on the ground, and it may
change where people need to be in order to support those
sorts of models.
Q. It's funny you should say that. I was talking to the
team the other day. I've just read a book called "The
patient will see you now" by someone called I think it's
Topol, a cardiologist in America. It was published in
2015, but it sort of predicts what you were just talking
about, the virtual assistant for your health care would be
widely available by now, which we're not quite there,
I don't think, although we can wear rings and watches that
monitor various of our - our heart rates and those sorts of
things and our sleep. But that book is very much
predicting the sort of virtual assistant particularly for
monitoring a chronic condition and all sorts of solutions
that you were just talking about. Have you come across
that book yourself?
A. I have not, and I will - I'll seek to find it. I'm
very interested in making sure that we're open to the way
health care is going to go, and unless - and I guess my
personal concern is and my focus is on equity. I think
these changes will be fabulous for rural and remote
citizens. But in order for them to have access we will
need ubiquitous broadband, and we will need the co-design
or the influence of people who live in rural communities.
But it's coming, and we - you know, 2048, general practice
is going to look a lot different.

Q. Yes, yes.
MR GLOVER: Consideration of expansion of scope of
practice or in providing environments where clinicians can
operate to the top of scope of practice apply equally
across other specialists as well in addition to GPs, do
they not?
A. Absolutely. And the changes will be as rapid in
non-GP specialist practice as specialist practice, and
that's what I was alluding to. I think you'll find this
absolute explosion in opportunities for different
treatments, for much more detailed - individually detailed,
genomically profiled treatments, and that will - so we have
to accommodate it as we're looking forward in this health
system to see how access will be organised to what are
going to be highly specialised scopes of practice.
One of my challenges, and you'll see this in my
statement, is that maintaining a generalist specialist
focus in our regional centres - and when I say regional
centres I'm talking about Wagga, Albury, Dubbo, Nowra,
Tamworth, Armidale, Coffs Harbour, Port Macquarie, our
regional centres that act as a hub-and-spoke model. Now,
at the moment we're asking the specialists in those areas
to be what I call specialist generalists, so to again have
a wider scope of practice than many of their metropolitan
colleagues, who are able to subspecialise and become, you
know, super expert in quite narrow scopes of practice.
Now, maintaining that focus certainly for the next
five to 10 years appears to me absolutely crucial if we're
to keep our health system running efficiently and not
expecting that we're going to be referring very large
numbers of patients centrally for care.
Q. I'll come back to this a little later, but one of the
priorities of the National Medical Workforce Strategy is to
build the generalist capacity. That includes both general
practitioners and general clinicians within hospitals;
correct?
A. Correct.
Q. Why is it important to build the general clinician
capacity within hospitals, in your view?
A. So, just as I've alluded to, in regional centres
subspecialty practice is challenging. Because being on

call is such a major aspect of the delivery of health care
in regional centres, if you are a subspecialist are we
going to have that person on call 24/7 seven days a week or
are we going to have a generalist physician on call taking
people from the area with heart attacks, strokes, you know,
sore tummies and then those being handed on to
subspecialists when and if appropriate. So the demands of
the on-call nature of those regional centres, where we
cannot - we do not have a critical mass of subspecialists
for every single specialty, then that's where I see the
generalist specialist workforce as really important.
So it's an issue in general surgery. It's an issue in
medicine. It's an issue in paediatrics. It's an issue in
obstetrics. We need people who have a wide scope of
practice across the continuum of their specialty because we
need them to be able to manage the sorts of emergencies
that come in from a catchment or a hub-and-spoke model
close to their regional centre.
Q. Is there also a need to build a generalist clinician
workforce within metropolitan hospitals?
A. Well, I believe so, and I believe so on the basis of
efficiency. So my question is generalists can manage
probability and manage uncertainty, whereas the more
specialist you are the more filtered, if you like, your
patients need to be and the lesser capacity to manage
across the continuum and particularly with patients with
multi-morbidity or chronic and multiple problems.
So, if you come into hospital under the respiratory
physician because you've got a cough but in fact your
urological plumbing isn't so good or your kidneys aren't
working so well, the whole concept of being able to be
managed with a generalist approach and prioritising those
issues - and I guess that's what geriatricians do with our
over 65-year-olds. In other words, they're not
specialising in one system. They're providing that
holistic overlook and prioritising the issues for the
patient's quality of life and outcome.
Q. Can I take you back to your statement, please, and to
paragraph 30.
A. Yes.
Q. Whilst we're on the topic of GPs, in paragraph 30 you
tell us there's a need to support rural general practice

and primary care to reduce unnecessary usage of acute
facilities, and then in the next sentence you tell us
recent collaborations around urgent care would appear
useful in this shared approach. What are the
collaborations that you're referring to, firstly?
A. So the urgent care program announced - there was two
urgent care programs announced, one through the
Commonwealth and one through the state jurisdiction. Now,
I guess this is one of the first initiatives that talks
about shared responsibility or shared concern about timely
access. So I guess it's a recognition that there has been
an increase in waiting time and patients visiting emergency
departments, and I guess this to me represented an effort
to consider access from the patient's point of view and try
and find a way forward.
So, whilst I'm not suggesting that I - that the model
might be - and the model is different as it's been applied
depending on who the jurisdictional - where the funding is
coming from. I think the idea of collaborating and
understanding the impact of primary care - the inability of
primary care currently to provide timely access is welcome
if it increases the collaboration between the two sectors.
Q. And do you see scope for further collaboration on that
issue?
A. I do. I think there are some preconditions which are
around data sharing and I guess the building of trust
between the two sectors to ensure that it's patient centred
and that it's relatively seamless. We could face an issue
where with notes not being shared there was extensive
duplication, and that feedback and that - yes, feedback to
primary care from specialty care I think needs to be
enhanced in order for these models to move forward.
Q. In paragraph 31 you tell us that there's further scope
for the LHDs to support access to primary care, and you
give an example in paragraph 32 of extending work locations
to have LHD-employed clinicians routinely attend community,
aged care and primary care settings; do you see that?
A. I do.
Q. Just in practice how might that work?
A. So the concept that you could second an employee of
New South Wales Health, perhaps someone skilled with
chronic disease management or interested in supporting a
chronic disease program that has a preventive focus, those

people could be situated in general practice as opposed to
link into general practice.
I think the other area that I think is ripe for
support is LHD health service professionals who are
involved in scopes of practice related to aged care, is in
reaching to provide care within aged care settings, and
there are some really excellent programs that have been
piloted looking at that exchange of personnel. But, again,
it comes down to communication and that approach of being
able to effectively data share and work as a
multidisciplinary team.
Q. And do you see initiatives like that as being one
lever that might be pulled to ensure the community has
access to the type of care they need within the community,
firstly?
A. I do, and I would welcome such initiatives. It is of
concern to me that, without that consideration of the
health system as a whole, presentations to acute facilities
may continue to rise.
Q. You've anticipated the next part of my question. Do
you see that as having a positive effect on keeping people
out of emergency departments who may not need to be there?
A. I do, and I welcome - so if I think about what works
well in rural and regional, and I'll go to small rural
because I think that's probably a better - the earlier you
can intervene and the more seamless your intervention, and
particularly if there is continuity of care or continuity
of management, then I think the outcomes are better. So if
we can link up those initiatives particularly around
prevention then I do believe that that will work to the
patient's benefit and I do think that will avoid
hospitalisations in the long run.
Q. Can I take you to paragraph 14 of your statement,
please, and in this section of your statement you identify
some potential solutions to the workforce challenges that
we've been discussing. We've touched on some of them, in
particular grow-your-own type initiatives. In paragraph 16
you tell us:
To support the system, training needs to
occur outside acute hospitals to ensure
that we are training the whole workforce we
need.

Could I just invite you to expand on the concept that
you're drawing to the Commissioner's attention in that
sentence?
A. So I'm specifically drawing your attention to the fact
that medical training in particular is very hospital
focused and yet we have this expectation that 50 per cent
or more of the trainees involved in postgraduate year 1 and
2 training within our hospitals will end up in the
community. It is of concern to me that the exposure of
those - both students and postgraduate year 1 and 2
trainees, if their exposure is not to community settings,
then I think it reduces the chance of them being positively
disposed to careers in that direction.
So as one of the ways of training the workforce we
need, which is more than just the people who are going to
have a hospital-based practice, then the better exposure
and the better training that reaches out from acute
hospitals I believe would better place trainees to take on
some of those careers.
Anecdotally, talking to trainees who are in hospitals,
leaving the hospital is a leap of faith, and particularly
if they have not been exposed to much primary care or
community-based practice then it is obviously more enticing
to look at a salaried hospital job that will lead to a
consultant position in a specialist - or following a
specialist training program.
Q. Are there any initiatives, either current or former,
that you're aware of that have been directed to that
particular issue?
A. Yes, and over time some of those initiatives have come
and gone, and, as I mentioned, the lead time for our
training - medical training in particular - is so long that
we're reaping the benefits or disbenefits of initiatives
that occurred 10 years ago, because it takes that long from
the medical student end for people to enrol in training
programs and finish their training and end up in a location
of choice or otherwise.
So some of those initiatives relate to primary care,
and there was a program way back called the PGPPP which
rotated trainees, PGY1 and 2 trainees, into general
practice. That ceased a number of years ago. But when
I talked to some of my current GPs they - many of them were

on or had terms like that and were positively disposed.
We now have the John Flynn training program, which is
rurally focused, and we've had considerable success locally
in identifying and supporting terms in Scone, Gloucester,
Moree, and we're just hoping to get a term like that up at
Manilla Hospital, and the reason for that is expressly to
expose our trainees to those locations and to that style of
practice with a hope of incentivising them to undertake
rural generalism or rural general practice as a career.
THE COMMISSIONER: The PGPPP has come up or has been
mentioned in some of our various regional site travels.
What did it stand for again?
A. Post - can't remember.
Q. Take that on notice.
A. I'll get back to you. Prevocational --
Q. We'll find out. Don't worry.
A. Prevocational general practice training program,
I think.
Q. What did it involve again? What was --
A. So it was a 10-week term rotation into general
practice.
Q. Yes.
A. And it occurred both metro and rural. It was
available across the state. The Commonwealth provided the
funding for it to backfill the positions. So New South
Wales Health was able to release those residents into
general practice terms.
Q. And it has been spoken of - well, the only time it's
come up, the person talking about it has spoken about it in
positive terms. When I asked - in terms of its benefit.
When I've asked why did it end I think I was told it ended
when a government ended and new government came in. Was
there any more to it than that as to why it ended?
A. I'm not aware of exactly why it ended. I think
programs such as that are expensive --
Q. Yes.
A. -- and it was - it was scale. So it was - those terms
were available to most trainees in the system, so --

Q. It sounded like it simply was a program that it didn't
end because it wasn't thought to be working; it ended
because the new government thought things had to be cut and
that was one of the things they cut?
A. I think there may have been a fiscal weighing up, yes.
Q. Yes. Okay. Thank you.
MR GLOVER: Do I take it from your experience and
understanding of that program, though, it was a beneficial
one to attracting clinicians to rural generalist practice?
A. Nearly - a large proportion of the GPs that I speak to
who are now, you know, 10 years into practice, they will
speak of that program being quite pivotal in their decision
to undertake general practice training.
THE COMMISSIONER: Perhaps I should make the generous
assumption that it wasn't cut because it was beneficial.
But who knows?
MR GLOVER: I won't say anything to that.
A. But I guess, Commissioner - I need to be careful - not
one particular - one initiative is going to fix this.
THE COMMISSIONER: No, of course not.
A. We've got a status issue for primary care and
generalism versus specialism that I've alluded to, we've
got a lack of exposure to community settings in some of our
university courses, and certainly in our postgraduate
training in hospitals, and we've got some salary and
remuneration issues, and we've got this whole thing about
generalism manages uncertainty and probability, and it's a
bit more messy, whereas specialty training, once you've
actually, you know, affirmed and got some really high-level
fabulous skills, you are in a position not to have to, you
know, accept some of the messiness that general practice
and deep-end general practice can have.
THE COMMISSIONER: I entirely accept, as you say, one
initiative is not going to fix this. But the fact that a
program is beneficial, it might mean that it costs a lot
and it's of benefit, but the benefit is either marginal or
it's better than marginal but it still costs a lot. But
the fact that a program is beneficial might also mean that
it should be scaled to a larger degree and, even though
it's expensive, you've got to weigh that with the benefit
it's producing and they might either net out or the benefit

might in the long term, given we're talking about health
care, actually far exceed the cost. Who knows?
A. Look, and to me --
Q. You won't know if you cut it, that's for sure.
A. Positive exposure is the key thing.
Q. Yes.
A. So the exposure's got to be positive because it's got
to entice. But my second point is, just in terms of
medical training, understanding the environment of general
practice and primary care, even if you end up in a
specialist training career, has to be beneficial that you
understand how the system works and you understand what it
is that the patients, you know, experience in the primary
care environment.
Q. Can I ask you this about the PGPPP - whatever quite
that means; we'll find out. Has it been replaced, in your
opinion, by a better program for exposing medical trainees
to general practice and in particular general practice in,
say, the regions?
A. So the John Flynn junior doctor prevocational training
program, or whatever its acronym is, has certainly been
beneficial from my perspective as someone who has been
involved in setting up some of those terms. But clearly
we've selected --
Q. It's a similar thing with a different name, is it, or?
A. I would think so.
Q. Yes.
A. So I feel that this is a really important program.
It's not at the same scale that PGPPP was.
Q. I see. Right.
A. So it's not as available.
Q. Yes.
A. But, again, anecdotally I hear very positive reports
of the exposure, and from my point of view, as I said,
people need to walk the walk and understand the environment
that they may be choosing to train for.
Q. Sure.
MR GLOVER: Considerations of that kind also apply to

training of specialist clinicians, do they not?
A. Correct, and that's why in I think it's section 16 I'm
drawing your attention to the importance if we understand
the need for having a distributed specialist workforce,
non-GP specialist workforce, and I suggest that their
presence in our regional centres is imperative to the
working of the New South Wales health system, that we need
to train people in those environments with a specific
understanding that that positive exposure again is likely
to be our major recruiter and our succession planner into
clinicians able to manage those roles.
Q. What needs to be done, in your view, to get to that
stage?
A. So the National Medical Workforce Strategy would
suggest that it is that really sincere collaboration
between colleges and the way that they design their
curriculums and the way that they value generalist skill
sets within colleges. It involves New South Wales Health,
and it involves probably a networking of training. But
we've got to decide whether we're going to prioritise those
locations for training and whether we are going to identify
that they get filled first and that they are an inreach
model or whether they were simply an outreach model from a
metropolitan centre, where obviously the focus is on
training for the scope of practice that can be seen in that
specialty training centre.
Q. By inreach and outreach do you mean inreach in the
sense that the trainee is primarily located in the regional
location?
A. Correct.
Q. And goes to the metro to the extent necessary?
A. Yes.
Q. As opposed to how it is at least weighted at the
moment, with the majority of specialist training occurring
in metropolitan regions with perhaps some short time in the
regions?
A. Exactly.
Q. You spoke of collaboration, and that is a key feature
or theme within the National Medical Workforce Strategy.
What can be done, if anything, to improve that process of
collaboration, given the fragmented nature of the system?
A. I think the most positive thing for me was that

states, all the jurisdictions, the Commonwealth, the
colleges, the medical schools and many of the industrial
bodies all endorsed the National Medical Workforce
Strategy. So at that level I appreciate that we have a
shared vision, a common goal in rebalancing some of the
aspects of our workforce in order to achieve a better
distribution.
On that basis, the issues relate to what colleges see,
and often appropriately so, are accreditation barriers,
supervision barriers. Some of that is related to the need
to rethink some of those things with virtual care and other
modalities. But I think it's that prioritising about what
is it that the whole system wants.
So I absolutely understand that where you have a
metropolitan training program and where you have a high
volume and a high population and a high density of work
that having someone out in the periphery perhaps with a
slightly different scope of practice and different
supervision arrangement, but what we've got to do is make
that everybody's main business. I think it has to be a
collaboration, and I think even me talking about it today
and putting it on the Commission's radar is I think about
trying to get those levers in order and get that greater
focus on regionalised training.
Q. Do the system managers of the state and territory
health systems have a role to play in engaging with the
colleges to rethink how training might be delivered outside
of metropolitan areas?
A. Absolutely.
Q. And do you see there to be a larger role that they
could be playing than is currently the case?
A. I do, and I understand that it is that the - if you
think about it, that the rural LHDs are a smaller voice
potentially in this than the metropolitan LHDs.
Q. So coordination --
A. A quieter voice, maybe.
Q. Coordination of effort not only is required at the
national level but at the state and territory
jurisdictional level; correct?
A. That's correct. And it's a prioritisation. It's
saying, "This is what we need to do if we want a workforce

for the future, and that means that we prioritise those
posts and we prioritise that as part of the network. They
should be filled first and they should be given the status
they need," and that involves things like the right sort of
inreach to get the skills to pass the training programs,
and, as I said, that's a whole of - a whole effort that
involves not only the colleges but the jurisdictions and
the - I guess, the importance placed on that sort of
training aim.
Q. And from your earlier observation do I take it that
you are of the view that individual rural LHDs or their
equivalents across the country are perhaps not best placed
to achieve that as opposed to a whole-of-jurisdiction type
approach?
A. They need help.
Q. I'll come to the detail - some of the detail of the
National Medical Workforce Strategy in a moment, but just
finally can I take you ahead to paragraph 36 of your
statement, please, and there you tell us that most LHDs are
facing population pressure and aging population, changing
consumer expectations and expanding health horizons. In
that is an increased prevalence of chronic disease;
correct?
A. Correct.
Q. Where you refer to changing consumer expectations what
did you have in mind?
A. I think there's been a change in what some of our
consumers regard as access, and I'll use the watch example.
Now that you can have a watch on your arm and that that
tells you that you might have a little funny heartbeat,
that now means - well, that's obviously raised a level of
anxiety and expectation of care that is somewhat greater
than it used to be. So I think as diagnostics moves closer
to the patients we've also got these changing expectations
about how we should be fulfilling them, and how accessible
and timely our health service might need to be. So it's a
comment on primary care as opposed to secondary care. But
obviously there's an overflow into secondary care as a
result.
I think the other thing is that we've seen a lot of
change related to changing policies, and what I mean by
that is with the advent, for instance, of the National
Disability Insurance Scheme we've seen a real need for

patients to access paediatric assessment services to
understand their eligibility, for instance, for entry into
the NDIS.
Now, parents would see that as time critical because
there is very good evidence that early intervention is
important with developmental conditions. So that's now put
quite a significant pressure on the system and a change in
expectations of those parents who are looking to try and
adequately access a whole plethora of assessment services
in order to seek the care that they need.
So it's all of those things that are in many ways
external to the delivery of the health system that I think
are changing, and that's what I meant by changing consumer
expectations.
Q. How might expectations of that kind be taken into
account in service and workforce planning activities?
A. I think it's very challenging. I think there's been a
reticence to identify, and this is related to rural areas,
a baseline level of access to services, and I share the
reticence, because obviously the reason to define it is to
then say that - or to then understand where the gaps are,
where that isn't being delivered, but the other concern for
me is that the baseline is changing. So how are we going
to keep up with a changing expectation in particularly the
timeliness of access, and, as I said, that's one of the
things that I'm thinking moving forward is going to be a
real challenge, and that's why I allude to the challenges
in scoping demand, for instance.
Q. Is one part of responding to that challenge in health
services engaging in conversations with their communities
about the level of service that might be able to be
delivered and delivered safely in particular areas?
A. Indeed. And the method of that service delivery, and
I'm alluding to the need to staff some emergency department
in our district hospitals and in our areas with virtual
emergency services, and the challenge for some of our rural
residents around that access and, as you said, the
conversations with the community about what is acceptable,
affordable and available access.
Q. Dealing with that example that you raised, do you
think there could be improvements as to how those
conversations are had at the moment?

A. I welcome those conversations. They're difficult
conversations. And, you know, I'm someone who has grown up
in a medical system where I was taught about humanity in
health and the laying on of hands. And I think that there
are also generational differences in the acceptability of
some of the care options that are on the table in rural New
South Wales. And I think those conversations are relevant,
but I do understand that they're difficult.
Q. Difficult conversations but important ones
nonetheless?
A. Yes.
Q. And important to engage in regularly?
A. And to be transparent about those conversations.
Q. What do you mean --
A. That they are trade-offs and, you know, that what's at
play in having - you know, in those decisions.
Q. By trade-offs, tell me if this is an example of
something you had in mind; that perhaps there is an
emergency department at a small rural facility that does
not see a high volume of patients both as to number and
acuity but, if that funding was diverted to dialysis
chairs, the needs of the community might be able to be
better met in a safe way; is that what you have in mind,
something like that?
A. That's exactly what I had in mind and it's that
transparency about that trade-off and that trade-off being
visible.
Q. We've heard in other hearings that the rural
population doesn't necessarily expect everything to be on
their doorstop and they accept some of the limitations. Is
that also your perception?
A. That is absolutely correct. So when I'm in Moree they
don't say to me, "Why haven't I got a cancer centre in
Moree, you know, and a PET scanner." There is an absolute
understanding that some of these services do need to be
centrally or regionally delivered. What I think consumers
want is access to adequate and reasonable health care
commensurate with the health needs of the community. So
those residents in Moree are delighted because they've got
a chemotherapy service that's working out of that
particular town. So their sick patients don't need to go
regionally; they can be managed locally. So it's that sort

of conversation that leads to outcomes that are clear and
obvious to the community.
Q. Can I take you now to the National Medical Workforce
Strategy. If you have a hard copy there, Professor?
A. I do. Well, I've got some of it, yes.
Q. All right. I'll have it brought up on the screen.
It's previously been tendered as exhibit H26 but it's also
attachment D, I think it is, to the professor's statement.
And, Professor, you were the co-chair of the Medical
Workforce Reform Advisory Committee that was involved in
the preparation of this strategy; correct?
A. Correct. I was just about to tell you that, so that
I have a very significant interest in this document.
Q. All right.
A. And I have been involved closely in its development.
Q. I don't need to ask you whether you're familiar with
it then. That role of co-chair was because you were the
representative of the National Rural Health Alliance on
that committee; is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. Can you just tell us a little bit about the alliance?
A. So the alliance is a fascinating organisation. It's
an alliance of up to about 40 organisations whose member
bodies have significant interests in rural and remote
health. It ranges between professional organisations, and
I was the Rural Doctors of Australia representative on the
National Rural Health Alliance, but also involves
organisations that are involved in health but not directly.
So we've got the Isolated Parents Association, we've got
the CWA, we've also got provider organisations such as
RFDS, Frontier Nursing, and Aboriginal organisations such
as the national community controlled sector and
representatives of nursing, allied health and other bodies.
So the great thing about the National Rural Health
Alliance is that its interests are more sector issues, not
professional issues between, you know, doctors and
mid-wives or whatever, whatever; but there are things about
bringing the sector forward. So they've been very
interested over the years in the provision of broadband,
ubiquitous broadband, to rural areas because we know that

that's a precondition for the availability of health care,
particularly going forward, and involved in issues such as
trying to determine the minimal level of standard of health
service care that I've just mentioned. So those are the
sorts of very useful contributions that the National Rural
Health Alliance have been able to make to the rural sector.
Q. And there were a number of members of this committee,
weren't there, the Medical Workforce Reform Advisory
Committee?
A. No. So the Medical Workforce Advisory Committee is
made up of the jurisdictions, the universities, the
industrial organisations such as AMA doctors in training.
Now it's also - since it's been reformed as MWRAC, it's
also got quite a lot of worker type bodies on it and
nursing and midwifery and allied health representation.
But the national Medical Workforce Advisory Committee, when
I was co-chair, which was - I finished on 30 June 2024, our
major effort was to develop this strategy, and that was
done, as I said, because the players from across the sector
were at the table.
Q. Thank you. And, Commissioner, for your benefit,
there's a list of committee members on page 73.
THE COMMISSIONER: 73, yes.
MR GLOVER: In general terms, Professor, acknowledging
that this was a significant piece of work, can you just
describe the process that was engaged in to develop the
strategy?
A. So the process occurred over about three years.
Initially there was some scoping and there was a consultant
brought in to, I guess, scope what the issues were. An
issues paper was generated which then went out to the
sector broadly, and then came back. And, again, the
membership of MWRAC was absolutely key to the development
of the strategy because it does straddle the myriad of
organisations that have levers in our medical workforce
training and development.
And then as a result of the workforce strategy there
were some specific pieces of work also that occurred, one
being looking at the service registrar group, who are a
group in our medical workforce that was identified as not
being on anybody's radar, I guess, initially. So this is a
group of clinicians who haven't chosen any specialty

training pathway and who are working often in hospitals,
and often in private hospitals. And the concern was did
they have - were they a homogeneous group and what were
their likely long-term intentions or were they a group that
should be supported to, I guess, remain and stay as, if you
like, a hospitalist, stay with a career in a hospital that
didn't involve a vocational outcome. That's just an
example of one of the working groups that occurred. And it
came back and it was for revision by all members of MWRAC,
and then it was finally endorsed, I think, end of 2022.
Q. Yes. I'll come back to the service registrars in a
moment, but can I take you - you'll see in the bottom
corners of the pages there some page numbers, and if I go
to page (vi), which is the foreword by the then secretary
of the Commonwealth department. If you don't have it in
the hard copy, the operator will bring it on the screen.
A. Yes.
Q. Thank you. And, Operator, if we scroll down a little
because the passage I want to take the professor to extends
over the page. So keep going. Yes. Just there. Thank
you.
Professor, can I invite you to read the paragraph
starting, "Implementation of this strategy" just to
yourself and let me know when you've done that.
A. Yes.
Q. These are the words of the then secretary, but do
I take it you agree with the concepts that he's describing
there?
A. Absolutely.
Q. And do you see in the last line on (vi):
In particular, specialist trainee numbers
can no longer be primarily driven by
clinical service requirements for
registrars that dominant many current care
models.
Do you see that?
A. Yes.
Q. Do you understand the concept to which he was
referring there?

A. I do. He was really referring to the increase in
annual compound growth in some of the specialist training
numbers which is so much greater than that into our
generalism or our general practice training numbers.
Q. And is the concept that that growth is driven by the
need to fill positions as opposed to the need to deliver
that particular type of care to the community?
A. That is one of the drivers.
Q. Can I take you ahead in the strategy to page 20,
please. I want to take you to some parts of this page,
Professor, but if you just take a moment to refresh your
memory about it and let me know and, if you need more time
to read it, at any stage just let me know?
A. No, I'm happy for you to ask.
Q. All right. In a couple of your earlier answers you've
mentioned status of generalist practice, and on this page a
number of suggestions are made as to what medical
leadership can do to address some of those issues. Who
would you put in the category of medical leadership in this
context?
A. That is such a good question.
Q. I'm glad I got one out.
A. That's very challenging.
Q. For the transcript, the Commissioner gave me a thumbs
up.
A. Traditionally, I would say it's the industrial
organisations, it's the Australian Medical Associations,
it's probably, you know, Rural Doctors Association. So
I think they are certainly key to changing the culture.
But I have to say that I think leadership in hospitals and
in hospital networks also need to have that helicopter view
which is that the health system will benefit if we're
training more generalist doctors and generalist doctors
that will have roles and responsibilities outside the acute
health system. So, whilst I understand the need and the
preference for training in the acute sector and for the
acute sector, clearly we need to increase the status of
generalism and general practice if we are to better
distribute our population - our medical workforce.
Having said that, unfortunately it is the attitude of
our students and our junior doctors who have heard or taken

on some of that bias, I guess, towards subspecialty
training and hospitally based training because of their
exposure or because it is a bias that we see significantly
in the medical community.
Q. Is there anything that the state and territory health
systems can do to overcome that perception and bias?
A. I believe so. I wonder - well, I'll just give you an
example. If you are a VMO on a fee for service rate in a
hospital you're paid, I don't know, $285 an hour or
whatever the going rate is. I'm not across because
I haven't claimed. The GP rate is somewhat lower. So,
I mean, you've got a message straight out there that a
consultant general practitioner is worth less than a
specialist practitioner. I would ask if they're doing a
job that is of significant benefit to the health system why
is there a difference.
Q. So what you have in mind is creating positions or
conditions that recognise the benefit of rural generalist
practitioners in those areas as a method of perhaps
overcoming some of that stigma; is that right?
A. Indeed, and levelling the playing field. And that
will not be lost on our medical students and junior
doctors.
Q. Is that because of a perception that rural generalism
or general practice is not a true specialty compared to
other subspecialties?
A. I guess so. It's certainly assumed to be less
valuable.
Q. On that page, the second dot point, do you see there:
There is a stigma about medical practice in
rural and remote Australia.
A. M'hmm.
Q. Is that something that you've observed?
A. Absolutely, and we have a term for it now. We call it
geographic narcissism.
Q. Again, is there anything that the state and territory
health systems can do to overcome that geographic
narcissism, in your view?
A. Absolutely. Absolutely. And it's the perception

that, if you work in the country, you mustn't have been
able to make it in the city. You know, I live in Tamworth.
Well, couldn't I get a job in the city? There is this - a
lot of it is not - like many sort of biases, it's not
malicious. It's not - it's just an assumption made that
the quality of the care or the service provision must be of
second grade or lesser than the opportunity in the city.
Now, in terms of opportunity, so say we take something
like lab based research, well, there's absolutely no doubt
that if you want to be involved in expensive and research
that requires large amounts of infrastructure that will not
be reproducible in anywhere outside a large metropolitan
centre. And so if that's the career of need then clearly
then the importance is that you locate and you champion
that career. What we've got to be careful of is that
inadvertently by general practice and generalism not being
seen in an acute facility that there's a necessary bias
that it's of lesser value.
Q. The third dot point on that page speaks of the need to
invest in understanding and championing cultural safety, in
particular in the context of growing the Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander workforce; do you see that?
A. I do.
Q. Is that a particular need in rural and regional
locations?
A. It is a particular need in rural and remote locations,
